title:
Seeing a color is not
the same as feeling it
lede: Questions and answers on The Grue Divide: When Cognitive Accuracy Doesn’t Predict Affective Alignment.

items.question: What is Color Fish Test?
answer: It’s the web platform we used to collect the data for The Grue Divide. In one session, participants count the blocks in blue color gradients (Study 1: perception), then describe a color scene in their own keywords (Study 2: emotion). At the end they get a playful “Color Fish” type as a thank-you.
After filtering, the analysis covers 9,534 trials from 1,159 participants: 904 Korean speakers living in Korea and 255 English speakers living in the US, UK or Australia.

items.question: What is the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis?
answer: Named after linguists Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, it says the language we speak influences how we think.

The strong version (linguistic determinism) says language fixes what we can perceive. Most researchers reject it. The weak version (linguistic relativity) says language nudges attention, memory and categorization. Color is a classic testing ground: Russian speakers discriminate blues faster when two shades cross the siniy/goluboy boundary (Winawer et al., 2007).

items.question: Why did this paper focus on Grue?
answer: One word, two colors. The Korean adjective pureuda covers both blue and green: haneul-i pureuda (“the sky is blue”) and soop-i pureuda (“the forest is green”). Koreans even call the green traffic light paran, usually “blue”, just as Japanese calls it ao shingō, the “blue signal”.

Blue is the anchor. In Obangsaek, the traditional five cardinal colors, blue stands for the East, wood and spring. The native word for blue, parang, has no Chinese-character equivalent, whereas the everyday word for green, chorok, is a Sino-Korean loanword.

Few forms, most used. Of the core Korean color categories, Grue has the fewest derivational variants, yet it is the one people produce most often in spontaneous language: in over 42,000 free-recall responses (Lee and Kim, 1996). A category that is lexically economical but cognitively salient is a good place to look for cross-linguistic differences.

Nuance packed into a single word. Korean builds shades from one root with prefixes, suffixes and vowel shifts, for example sae-paran (vivid blue), pureu-jukjuk (dull, sickly blue-green) and paran → peoreon (bright → dark, somber blue). English mostly uses phrases instead (dark blue, bluish green).

items.question: What did you find?
answer: Perception: Korean speakers made fewer counting errors than the English-speaking cohorts (median error score 0.056 vs. 0.147). The gap is significant within the Grue spectrum and also pooled across all color categories. The effect is small (see Statistical rigor).

Emotion: in the “Australia Divergence”, Korean and Australian participants were statistically equivalent in accuracy. Yet in how they described colors emotionally, Australians grouped with the US and UK, not with Korea. Seeing a color boundary with the same precision doesn’t mean feeling it the same way: a cognitive–affective decoupling.
The Australian subsample is small (132 trials), so we present this as an illustrative case for future confirmatory work, not a definitive claim.

items.question: What is the SFF framework?
answer: SFF turns each free-text keyword into a three-dimensional vector: Sentiment (valence), Formality (social distance) and Friendliness (warmth). Gemini 2.5 Flash scores every keyword from −1.0 to 1.0 on each axis and returns the result as JSON.

Splitting Formality from Friendliness was informally motivated by Korean honorifics, where formal speech doesn’t by itself imply distance. People often use a formal register with close, familiar addressees in public settings.

items.question: How did you recruit so many participants?
answer: 1. Make something people want to try. People love a test that tells them something about themselves. So Color Fish Test lets you measure your own color perception and see your result, your Color Fish type, right away. Curiosity does most of the recruiting.

2. Keep the ads simple. We ran paid social ads, mainly on X. In the X Ads Manager, pick a campaign objective that optimizes for people engaging with or visiting your platform, then set your target audience. After that:
  • Check the numbers every day to see whether participation keeps rising.
  • Try switching the optimization goal (e.g., from clicks to views) and keep whichever metric performs best.
  • Use the AI-driven optimization options now built into ad tools. They can bring in noticeably more participants.
We also used Prolific, HelloTalk ads and unpaid LinkedIn posts. In total the ads reached over 339K people (EN 94K, KR 245K) for about €300.

items.question: Can I collect responses in Google Sheets without writing a backend?
answer: Yes. If you can’t build a server, Google Apps Script can turn a Google Sheet into a simple data endpoint. Each submission becomes a new row.

• Create a Google Sheet with a tab named responses and a header row.
  • Open Extensions → Apps Script and paste:

function doPost(e) {
  const sheet = SpreadsheetApp.getActiveSpreadsheet().getSheetByName('responses');
  const d = JSON.parse(e.postData.contents);
  sheet.appendRow([d.user_id, d.trial_number, d.actual_blocks,
                   d.user_estimate, d.duration_seconds]);
  return ContentService.createTextOutput('ok');
}

• Deploy → New deployment → Web app, with Execute as: Me and Who has access: Anyone. Copy the web app URL.
  • In your test page, send each trial when it’s submitted:

fetch('YOUR_WEB_APP_URL', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({ user_id, trial_number, actual_blocks,
                         user_estimate, duration_seconds })
});
Sending the body as plain text (the default for a string) avoids a CORS preflight, which Apps Script doesn’t answer.

Before you go live: anyone with the URL can post to it, so collect only anonymized data. If you log timestamps, remove them before sharing the dataset, as we did. For larger studies, a real database is sturdier, but a Sheet is plenty for a pilot.

items.question: What does the data pipeline look like?
answer: Each participant does both studies in one web session. The data then pass through one filter and split into a cognitive track and an affective track, which meet again at the end.
The LLM enters the pipeline only twice, to generate the scenes and to score keywords. It plays no role in Study 1.

items.question: How is accuracy measured?
answer: Each trial gets a difficulty-weighted relative error, R<sub>E</sub>: how far the guess is from the true count, relative to the count, and weighted by how hard the bar was.

Trials are grouped by color category (the gradient from blue to white, black, yellow or red), and the time spent on each trial is recorded too. Responses longer than 300 seconds (5 minutes) were removed as outliers.

Because the weights {1, 2, 3} are a convention, we re-ran the analysis under three alternative weightings and a fully rank-based measure. The Korean advantage and the KR ≈ AU pattern held every time. The rank-based measure correlates with R<sub>E</sub> at Spearman ρ = 0.971.

items.question: How big are the effects?
answer: What Cohen’s d measures. It tells you how far apart two groups’ averages are, in units of how spread out the data are (standard deviations). A rough guide: about 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.

Ours are small, and we say so plainly. For error rate, KR vs. all English-speaking participants gives d = 0.174; KR vs. UK is 0.200 and KR vs. US is 0.181. The rank-biserial correlation, r = 0.211, says the same thing without assuming normal data: pick one Korean trial and one English-speaking trial at random, and the Korean one has the lower error roughly 6 times in 10 (a coin flip would be 5).
In natural units, the English-speaking cohort’s error rate averages 1.16× the Korean cohort’s, a 14% lower error rate for Korean speakers, holding covariates fixed.
Why the p-values are tiny anyway: with thousands of trials, even a small, consistent difference is very unlikely to be chance. A small p-value tells you a difference is real, not that it’s big.

items.question: How do you show KR and AU are equivalent, not just “not different”?
answer: Why a normal test isn’t enough. A regular significance test can only say “we didn’t find a difference.” That isn’t the same as “there is no difference”, just as not finding your keys doesn’t prove they’re not in the house. With a small group like the Australian one (132 trials), a test can easily miss a real difference.

What TOST does instead. A Two One-Sided Test flips the question. First we decide how small a difference is too small to matter: here ±0.068 in error-rate units (see the box below). Then we test the difference from both sides at once: one test checks it isn’t too far below zero, the other that it isn’t too far above. Only if both pass do we call the two groups equivalent. A Bayes factor then checks the same question a different way.

Where does ±0.068 come from?

In real terms: on a 20-block bar at level 1, that’s a difference of about 1.4 blocks in the answer.

• Error rate: equivalent. TOST p = 0.003. A bootstrap 90% CI of the median difference, [−0.032, 0.025], falls inside the margin. A Bayes factor points the same way: BF01 ≈ 4.6, so the data are about 4.6 times more likely if there is no difference than if there is one (moderate evidence).
  • Response duration: not equivalent. TOST p = 0.625, BF10 = 2.96. Korean and Australian participants were about as accurate, but not about as fast.
The ±0.2 SD margin is the conventional “small effect” threshold, not one derived from our data. A stricter or looser margin could change the conclusion.

items.question: How did you handle age and other confounds?
answer: Age strongly predicts error: the 45+ group’s coefficient is β = 0.898, p < 0.001. So we reweighted the English-speaking cohort to match the Korean age distribution, with w(a) = P<sub>KR</sub>(a) / P<sub>EN</sub>(a).

The main model is a GLM with age group, color category, media type, weekly media hours and country. KR differs from the UK (p = 0.028) and US (p = 0.039) but not from AU (p = 0.973). Refitting with a different reference country gives identical contrasts, so the AU result isn’t an artifact of AU being the baseline.

items.question: What other robustness checks did you run?
answer:
• Zeros in the data: 34.3% of trials have RE = 0, which a Gamma GLM can’t formally represent. A Tweedie refit keeps the language effect stable (β = 0.132–0.146, p = 0.007–0.012 vs. Gamma β = 0.152).
  • Grue-only GLM: the effect points the same way but isn’t significant on its own (β = 0.218, p = 0.085; only 293 English trials). The Mann–Whitney test on the same subset is significant, so we treat the pooled model as the primary evidence.
  • LLM stability: re-scoring keywords at four temperatures gives median cosine similarity ≈ 0.99, with no significant instability after Bonferroni correction.

items.question: What are the main limitations?
answer:
• The study is exploratory and correlational: it generates hypotheses rather than establishing causes.
  • SFF scores come from an LLM and haven’t yet been validated against human raters. Sentiment and Friendliness are highly collinear (r ≈ 0.97–0.98).
  • The Australian subsample is small (132 trials).
  • Gender couldn’t be linked to the main Korean cohort, and ad delivery skewed over 90% female.
  • AI-generated scenes vary in content, so keywords may partly reflect the scene rather than the color.
  • Participant-level K-means clusters don’t separate by country (ARI ≤ 0.006). The country divergence comes from country-average SFF profiles.

items.question: Where can I find the data and code?
answer: The full dataset (N = 9,534), Model Card and Datasheet are on OSF. The experimental platform’s source code is on GitHub.
